prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in such moire systems

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B005 as my single-part preference, with the same three names and a citation confined to the prediction and the observed phenomena. What the first round clarified for me is that the committee is not divided on the quality of B005 and B007; the chair's summary shows that all eight accept both as high-level science and that the contest is about maturity and attribution. On that axis I weigh the two differently from the six B007 supporters. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity form a theory-and-nature pair of the kind a physics prize should reward, and the phenomenology has now been reproduced by many independent groups over about eight years and carried into other moire platforms. The field it opened is new matter with tunable parameters, not a higher-precision version of an existing measurement. I also note that several B007 supporters moved there after reading the openings, so the six-to-two count is not independent evidence of merit, and I do not treat it as one in either direction. My view is therefore a change in emphasis only: I now put more weight on keeping the B005 citation strictly descriptive, and I regard B007 as a fully defensible prize that I would accept without reservation about its science.
statement.case_against: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, twist-angle disorder complicates what is intrinsic, and the credit chain has a visible hole: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, cannot be named under the three-person limit and the supplied credited names, and earlier band-theory work on twisted layers (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and other moire experiments (Dean, Young, Yazdani) have claims a short citation cannot absorb. Five colleagues treat the Cao omission and the open mechanism as real obstacles, and I accept that a prize here will be criticised on attribution in a way a two-name clock prize would not. B007, by contrast, has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and a mature, reproduced 1e-18 result, with the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition of the second as its main reservations.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B007 for its compact attribution and measurable outcome, treats B005 as somewhat early because the pairing interpretation is unstable, and wants the B007 citation worded around magic-wavelength lattice trapping.
responses.response: I agree that a B007 citation worded around neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping would separate the achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and that Kroll's own Hall-laboratory connection does not require recusal. Where I still differ is on what maturity requires. A prize for B005 would reward the existence, tunability and reproducibility of flat-band, correlated-insulator and superconducting phases, all of which are established across many laboratories, and not a settled explanation of the pairing. Superconductivity in the cuprates was recognised on that logic in 1987, and I would hold B005 to the same standard. I do concede that Kroll's point about Ye's role beyond the first demonstration makes the two-name B007 attribution stronger than I allowed in round 1.

responses.point: Pearce calls B007 the natural runner-up if the committee judges twisted bilayer graphene larger, says the Cao omission and the open pairing mechanism could change his ordering, and gives weight to the independent agreement of the B007 assessments rather than the count.
responses.response: This is the most useful framing in the chair's own statement, and I accept it: the question is whether scale outweighs the credit gap. My answer is that the gap is a consequence of the three-person limit and not of any doubt about who made the discovery, since the 2011 prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero group's observation are clearly identifiable. I would not claim the Cao omission is costless, and if the committee judges it decisive I would support B007 as the fallback, which is why it is my first alternative. What I cannot support is treating the omission as a scientific demerit of the phenomena themselves, because it concerns who can be named, not whether the effect is real or reproduced.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B025 to B007 and, like Olsson, would credit B005 with only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, noting the maturity concern that recognition might be slightly early.
responses.response: The chair asks who would change if Bistritzer is dropped. I would not welcome it, because the continuum model that locates the magic angle and the flat bands is a joint 2011 result of Bistritzer and MacDonald, and a prize crediting only MacDonald would cut a single paper's authorship in a way that is hard to explain. If the committee found a two-name B005 the only acceptable form, I would still prefer it to B007, but I would regard it as the weaker attribution. On timing, I take Mehlig's point that the case would be easier in a few years, but waiting does not fix the Cao problem, so it is not a reason to prefer B007 this year.

responses.point: Johansson moved his preference from B044 to B007, arguing that lattice clocks turn gravitational redshift over millimetres into a laboratory observable and that the committee is better served by a mature, cleanly attributable candidate.
responses.response: I find the geodesy and redshift argument persuasive as physics and it moves B007 up in my own estimation, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. I would however separate the question of the clock's real scientific payoff from the question of timing: Johansson himself notes that the redefinition of the second is still pending and that the committee must word the citation to avoid rewarding accuracy in general. Those are two reservations on B007 that B005 does not share to the same degree. I also appreciate that he has disclosed his proximity to B044 and discounted his earlier view; that candidate should in any case be weighed with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize in mind.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers the same B005 trio, stresses the breadth of the moire family and flags field proximity to correlated-electron theory as a possible bias.
responses.response: I share the three-name configuration and the view that the platform's generality matters most. I would resist the suggestion in Eriksson's uncertainties that fractional Chern insulators and twisted WSe2 should be pulled into the citation; those developments are real but later and are better left out so the citation does not overreach. I also note that Eriksson and I are the only two preferring B005, so our shared reasoning should be tested and not taken as confirmation; the other six members' objections on attribution deserve a direct answer, which is what I have tried to give above.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the omission of Yuan Cao as decisive, which would make B007 the better choice this year.
Whether a citation limited to the prediction and the observation of the phenomena is read as appropriately modest or as evasive about the pairing mechanism.
Whether the lattice clock is judged a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; if so, B007 is as defensible as B005 on science.
I rely on recalled priority history for the 2011 and 2018 papers and for the lattice-clock chronology, and have not verified exact dates.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not appear among the credited names of B005, B007 or B001, and my research in string theory, de Sitter space and cosmology is not close to these topics. I note that Eriksson and I share a preferred configuration, and that this agreement should not be treated as independent confirmation.
